analysis.location_and_population: Bangladesh; study population: 341 children aged ≤14 years admitted to Bangladesh Shishu Hospital & Institute with suspected measles.
analysis.event: icddr,b, in collaboration with Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute, conducted a laboratory-confirmed investigation concluding there is no genetic evidence that the circulating measles virus has escaped vaccine-induced immunity.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Among 341 suspected cases, 324 were laboratory-confirmed measles; 142 of 146 infants <9 months (not yet eligible for vaccination) tested positive; 122 of 126 unvaccinated children tested positive; 44 of 48 children with one dose tested positive; 16 of 21 children with two doses tested positive. analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: icddr,b and partners are expanding genomic surveillance, launching a clinical cohort study across four divisional hospitals, enlarging birth-cohort immunology studies, piloting zinc adjunct therapy, and conducting community research on missed vaccinations; researchers emphasize that vaccination remains the most effective prevention and urge adherence to the national two-dose schedule; further population-based studies are needed to quantify vaccine effectiveness and explain outbreak spread despite high reported coverage.

analysis.brief_en: A study by icddr,b, in partnership with Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute, has found no genetic evidence that the measles virus currently circulating in Bangladesh has escaped protection from the existing measles-rubella vaccine. The investigation, which analyzed samples from 341 hospitalized children with suspected measles between 20 April and 21 May 2026, confirmed measles in 324 cases. Among infants under nine months—too young for vaccination—142 of 146 tested positive, while 122 of 126 unvaccinated children and 44 of 48 children who received only one dose tested positive. In contrast, 16 of 21 children who had received both recommended doses tested positive, indicating lower positivity among fully vaccinated children. Genetic analysis showed the virus belongs to genotype B3, with no evidence of vaccine escape despite the detection of four mutations in antibody-recognized regions of the H protein.
